subject: circuits

milestone.title: Series and parallel resistors
milestone.objective: Reduce a series-parallel resistor network to one equivalent resistance in under 5 minutes

sources.title: Course notes p.5 (fixture)
sources.text: Resistors in series carry the same current. Their equivalent resistance is the sum: Req = R1 + R2 + ... Resistors in parallel have the same voltage across them. Their equivalent resistance satisfies 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ... For two resistors this is Req = R1 R2 / (R1 + R2). The equivalent resistance of a parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest resistor in it. Example: 100 ohm in parallel with 400 ohm gives Req = 100 x 400 / 500 = 80 ohm. To reduce a network, combine the innermost series or parallel groups first and work outwards.

lesson_lines: Series resistors carry the **same current**. Add them: Req = R1 + R2 + …
Parallel resistors have the **same voltage** across them. Use 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …, or for two resistors the product over sum: Req = R1 R2 / (R1 + R2).
A useful check: the equivalent resistance of a parallel combination always lies between the smallest and the largest resistor.
Combine the innermost series or parallel groups first, redraw, and work outwards until one resistor is left.
Reduce: 220 Ω in series with (330 Ω ∥ 680 Ω). Give Req in Ω.

planted_errors.quote: always lies between the smallest and the largest resistor
planted_errors.correct: is always smaller than the smallest resistor
planted_errors.why: The source says a parallel Req is always smaller than the smallest resistor.
